Convention note — header This <header class="page-header"> block is copied byte-for-byte from every other applet (see conventions.md § Header). Never redeclare .page-header h1/h2 locally, and never swap the real anchor tags for a <p> — screen-reader users rely on the page having exactly one <h1>/<h2> pair here, and it doubles as a working link back to the department site and the app index.
Convention note — landmarks Everything specific to this page — the lesson card, the interactive widget, the reflection guide — lives inside one <main>. There is exactly one <main> per page. <header> is reused site chrome, so it sits outside <main>. Each distinct region inside main (.lesson-container, .app-wrapper, .reflection-container) is a <section> with aria-labelledby pointing at that section's own visible heading id — never a bare <div>, and never aria-label duplicating text that's already visible on screen.

Activity 0T: How This Applet Was Built

Learning Objectives

  • Identify the four page regions every applet uses: page header, activity card, applet card, reflection guide.
  • Locate where the shared look-and-feel (colors, fonts, card styling) is defined versus where page-specific widget CSS belongs.
  • Apply the id / aria-labelledby pairing rule when labeling a new section.

Background

Every LING2150 applet is a single static HTML file (plus, optionally, a page-specific CSS/JS pair) that loads the shared docs/style.css. That shared stylesheet supplies the card look, the color palette, the fonts, and a handful of reusable widgets (buttons, a stage-rack, a feedback card). A page's own CSS should only add what is genuinely specific to its own interactive widget — this page's widget gallery below shows both kinds side by side.

Instructions

  1. Scroll through the fake applet below like a student would.
  2. Read the blue "Convention note" callouts next to each part — they explain the rule that part demonstrates.
  3. When you're ready to build your own page, copy this file, delete the callouts and the banner, and replace the content.
Convention note — no shrinking substantive text Learning Objectives, Instructions, and the Reflection & Discussion Guide are course content the student is meant to read, same as Background — don't add class="small" to their lists or wrap it around them. If you want a lighter visual touch, that's what uga-accent headings and generous line-height already provide.

Widget gallery

Two working demo widgets, a button set, and two optional callout patterns — copy whichever pieces your activity actually needs.

Convention note — applet title The <h2 id="applet-title"> above lives inside .hero/ .hero-text, both defined once in style.css. The id here must match the aria-labelledby on the <section class="app-wrapper"> that contains it — that's what gives a screen reader user a named landmark to jump straight to the interactive part of the page.

📖 Extra terminology (optional)
  • Landmark: a region of the page (header, main, nav, ...) that assistive technology lets a user jump directly to.
  • Contrast ratio: a measure of how easy text is to read against its background; WCAG AA asks for at least 4.5:1 for normal text.

Compare this to Background/Instructions above, which are never collapsed — a student shouldn't have to click to reveal what they're supposed to do. <details> is for genuinely optional extras.

Convention note — chat Every applet that shows a conversation uses the same look: .chat-log (an <ol role="log">) holding .chat-turn items, with the role as a class — .human sits left in grey, .ai sits right in a teal tint. Each turn has a .chat-turn__speaker line that starts with its number ("1. You") so students can cite turns, and a .chat-turn__text bubble. Typing goes in .chat-compose (label + .chat-compose__row with the field and a send button). Apps with extra needs use the slots instead of inventing new chat CSS: .chat-turn__extras for a per-turn control (7B's "mark this turn" select, used on the first AI turn below), .chat-compose__extras for options that belong to the whole conversation (3B's auto-generate toggle, the checkbox below), a select placed inside .chat-compose__row (3_coref's speaker picker), .just-added to ring a new turn, .thinking + .thinking-dots for "AI is typing", and .chat-log--static for a fixed example that shouldn't scroll. For an editable list of turns (5C), use the .turn-row pattern instead.

    Convention note — form fields Wrap a label and its control in .field and it gets the site look (13px bold Merriweather Sans label, 15px control text, 44px minimum height). Put explanatory text in .field-hint, mark optional labels with .field-optional, and show validation problems in .error-text with role="alert". Lay fields out in a grid of your own; don't restyle the fields themselves.

    A hint sits under the control; use it for what the field is for or where the data goes.

    Convention note — buttons .btn-uga, .btn-uga-dark, .btn-uga-outline, and .btn-reset are all defined once in style.css (same font, size and 44px touch target, whether the button sits in a card or in a .stage-content) — reuse them instead of inventing a page-local button style. Group them in .btn-row; a row whose buttons are all hidden takes no space.

    Color palette

    All colors are CSS custom properties on :root in style.css — reference them with var(--name) rather than hard-coding a hex value, so a future palette change only has to happen in one place.

    --uga-red#ba0c2fPrimary accent: buttons, the left border on every card, active/error states.
    --olympic#004e60"Done"/success-adjacent state (e.g. a completed stage).
    --hedges#b4bd00Discussion-box tint. Text on it must stay dark (see contrast note below).
    --uni-blue#0055a4Used sparingly for a second categorical color (e.g. a speaker label).
    --sanford#554f47Muted heading text inside a tinted box.
    --panel-alt#f9f9f9Neutral surface for a stage-num circle, a glossary box, an inert control.
    --text#1a1a1aBody text.
    --muted#555555Secondary text (sub-labels, hints, timestamps).

    Accessibility notes

    • Landmarks: one <header> (site chrome), one <main> (this page's unique content), and a <section> for each distinct labeled region inside main. Don't reach for <section> for small internal wrappers like .hero or .chat-turn — those aren't destinations a screen-reader user would want to jump to on their own.
    • aria-labelledby over aria-label: when a section already has a visible heading, point aria-labelledby at that heading's id instead of duplicating the text in aria-label — one source of truth, and it stays correct if the heading text is edited later. Reserve aria-label for controls with no visible text, like an icon-only mic button.
    • Every aria-labelledby needs a real target: after editing any heading, grep the file for aria-labelledby="..." and confirm each target id still exists. This is the single easiest thing to silently break when restyling a heading.
    • Contrast: check any new color-coded badge or tinted box against WCAG AA (4.5:1 for normal text, 3:1 for large text/UI components) before shipping it. A real example from this codebase: 3_coref.html's "place" entity badge originally used white text on --lake-herrick teal (3.07:1 — fails AA); it was changed to dark text on the same teal (5.67:1) while keeping the swatch color itself unchanged.
    • Uppercase headings are CSS, not typed text: style.css applies text-transform: uppercase to every h1/h2/h3. Always type heading text in normal sentence/title case in your HTML and let CSS transform it visually — never type an actual all-caps string, which can read strangely to some assistive tech.
    • <details> is for optional content only: Background and Instructions must always be visible without a click — a student shouldn't have to discover that there's more to read. Reserve collapsible sections for genuinely optional extras, like the glossary box in stage 3 above.
    • Skip link (recommended): a <a class="skip-link" href="#main"> as the very first thing in <body>, paired with <main id="main" tabindex="-1">, lets a keyboard user jump straight past the repeated page header. It must actually become visible on keyboard focus (the shared .skip-link:focus rule does this) — a skip link that stays permanently hidden isn't usable by anyone.
    • Chat logs: give the .chat-log role="log" (or, when a separate role="status" line already announces each reply, just an aria-label) and tabindex="0" so a keyboard user can scroll it. Give every message box a real <label> — use .visually-hidden if the design has no room for a visible one, never a placeholder alone.

    Reflection & Discussion Guide

    Convention note — reflection guide Always a plain <ol>, no tinted callout box, and never class="small" — this is the same weight of content as everything else on the page, just placed at the end, outside the interactive area.
    1. Which widget above would you reuse for your own activity, and which would you skip?
    2. Look at this file's source. Which parts are the reusable pattern, and which parts (the banner, the blue callouts, the divider lines) exist only to explain the pattern and should be deleted when you copy this file?
    3. Pick one heading on this page and confirm its id matches the aria-labelledby of the section that contains it.
    Convention note — reflection notes If students can write anything down, use the one standard box, exactly as below: .reflection-notes (also a .field), the fixed label "Write down your thoughts", a textarea, a "Download my notes" button and the fixed note underneath. There is no extra prompt: students are simply answering the numbered questions above it. The download is always its own button, never merged into the applet's own download; it saves the guide's questions plus the notes as a text file, via the shared docs/reflection-notes.js (include it with <script src="../reflection-notes.js" defer>). If the applet also lets students export their work (chat transcripts, rewrites, marker data), put that button in the applet card, not here. 5C, 7A and 7B all use exactly this.

    Your notes stay in this browser and are not submitted to your instructor. Download them before you close this page.

    Convention note — feedback card (required) Every applet ends with this card, directly after </main>; it is how students and instructors report bugs and content errors. Copy the markup exactly. The three query parameters in the button's href — title, applet and source-url — must name this activity and its own page URL; a site-wide audit once found two pages that had copy-pasted the link from a third page and were mislabeling every bug report. Add applet-feedback-card--followed when another card (the source card below) comes after it.

    Sources & permissions

    Example credit line: Dataset or recording name, authors and contributors. Downloaded from the official archive (opens in a new tab). Released under a named license, with a link to it and a note of any changes made.

    Longer notes (optional)

    Clip details, model names, limitations and privacy notes go in collapsed <details> inside the card so the credit itself stays short.

    Convention note — source card Any applet that reproduces or adapts someone else's material (a benchmark, a corpus, recordings, a paper, a hosted model) credits it in a <footer class="source-card"> after the feedback card — not in a page-local card style and not buried in a <details> in the app. If the applet uses no third-party material, omit it.
